title: Vibe coding is easy. Finding demand isn’t.

Peter Njuguna 4 min read · Just now -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size From Nightly Build to Market Insight AI makes building easy, but demand is the hard part. Learn AI product validation so your next app solves a problem people will pay for. On a Friday night in Nairobi, a developer I’ll call Wanjiru opened her laptop with an idea: an app that helps small shop owners track stock and automatically remind customers who owe them money. By Sunday evening, it was done login, dashboard, SMS reminders, a clean logo. AI wrote most of the code she had never built something this fast. She posted a screenshot online, collected a few dozen likes, and went to bed feeling like she had just unlocked a superpower. Three months later, the app had 11 users. Two of them were her cousins. The new reality: building is no longer the hard part Something real has changed. A few years ago, building software meant months of learning, hiring or begging a developer friend for favours. Today, with vibe coding , no-code and low-code tools, and AI assistants, you can build a product with AI in a weekend. That is genuinely good news. More people can create. More ideas can become real. But it hides a trap. When building becomes cheap, everyone builds. The internet fills up with apps, tools and “AI-powered” everything. The scarce resource is no longer code. It is attention, and the willingness of a real person to open their wallet. The trap: easy to build is not the same as wanted Wanjiru did what most of us do. She fell in love with the solution before she understood the problem. Her thinking went: shop owners are disorganised, so they need an app. It sounded logical. But she had never asked a single shop owner how they tracked stock today. When she finally did, in month three, the answers surprised her. Most of them used a notebook. It was free, it worked, and they trusted it. The debt reminders she thought were genius? They preferred a phone call, because the relationship with the customer mattered more than efficiency. Her app solved a problem she imagined. Nobody had told her it was a problem at all. This is the build-first, validate-never mistake, and AI makes it more tempting than ever. When a weekend is all it takes, why bother asking questions first? Because the weekend isn’t the real cost. The real cost is the three months afterwards, when you’re marketing something nobody asked for and slowly deciding the world is wrong. The real bottleneck: should I build it? For years, the question was “Can I build it?” AI has largely answered that: yes, probably. The question that matters now is “Should I build it?” Finding a problem worth solving is the new scarce skill. It can’t be automated, because it lives in conversations, in observation, and in the uncomfortable work of asking strangers what annoys them and what they already pay to fix. Easy to build doesn’t mean there’s demand. The code was never the hard part. The hard part is caring about a problem enough to understand it, and finding people who care enough to pay. A practical framework for startup idea validation Here is what Wanjiru did on her second attempt. You can use it before your next build. Start with a painful, frequent, specific problem. “Small businesses struggle with money” is too vague. “Shop owners lose track of who owes them, and it costs them sales every month” is something you can test. Talk to 10 people before writing any code. Don’t pitch. Ask how they handle the problem today, what it costs them, and what they’ve tried. Look for existing spending. Workarounds, paid tools, hired helpers and wasted hours are signals. If people already spend money or time on a problem, demand exists. If they shrug, it doesn’t. Test willingness to pay early. Offer a pre-sale, a deposit or a paid pilot. A compliment costs nothing, but a payment is proof. Build the smallest version and watch what people actually do. Build an MVP , not a masterpiece. Measure real usage, not likes. This is how you move towards product-market fit : by listening first and building second. Mistakes to avoid Asking friends and family, who will be polite instead of honest Confusing “that’s cool” with “I’d pay for that” Adding features instead of finding customers Treating a finished build as a finished business Skipping the conversations because they feel awkward What happened to Wanjiru She shelved the app and spent a month talking to shop owners. She learned that their real headache wasn’t stock, it was the daily reconciliation of mobile money payments against what customers claimed to have paid. She built a very simple tool for exactly that. This time, 8 of the first 10 people she showed it to asked how much it cost. Same developer, same AI tools, same weekend of building. The only difference was that she started with a problem instead of a product. The takeaway AI has given all of us the power to build almost anything. That makes the old question more important than ever: does anyone need this? Before your next build, don’t open your editor. Talk to five people who have the problem. Their answers will tell you whether to build, what to build, or whether to walk away and save your weekend. What are you about to build, and who have you asked?
